summary: Defines a Service Location Protocol template that RSIP servers use to advertise their services. This lets clients discover an RSIP server on the network instead of being configured by hand. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a sign on a shop door that says what the shop offers, so people can find the right shop without being told.

subtitle: A service type template for advertising Realm Specific IP servers using Service Location Protocol.

tldr.problem: RSIP clients need to discover RSIP servers on their network, but manual configuration is cumbersome. There was no standard protocol for automatic RSIP server discovery.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3105 defines a Service Location Protocol (SLP) service type template that allows RSIP servers to advertise themselves with attributes describing their capabilities (tunneling methods, security support, current load), and clients to query for servers matching their requirements.
tldr.outcome: This experimental protocol describes how to use SLP (an existing IETF standards-track service discovery protocol) to solve the RSIP server discovery problem, enabling dynamic and load-aware server selection.

today: RFC 3105 is an Experimental protocol and has not been obsoleted. It describes how to use SLP, an existing standards-track protocol, to discover RSIP servers. The RSIP technology itself saw limited deployment; the IESG noted in RFC 3105 that RSIP requires significant host and gateway changes and may cause interoperability problems with some applications (notably IPsec).

sections.title: RSIP Server Discovery with SLP
sections.content:
RFC 3105 describes how to use the Service Location Protocol (SLP, RFC 2608) to enable Realm Specific IP (RSIP) clients to automatically discover RSIP servers. RSIP allows a client in one network realm to borrow addresses and resources from another realm via an RSIP protocol exchange with an RSIP server. Previously, clients had to know a server's address through manual configuration, DNS SRV records, DHCP, or other static methods.

SLP is an IETF standards-track protocol designed for dynamic service discovery. It allows services to advertise themselves (via a Service Agent) and clients to query for services (via a User Agent). This document specifies the service type template that defines how RSIP servers should advertise themselves and what attributes clients should be able to query.
sections.plainLanguage: RSIP servers can now broadcast 'I am an RSIP server with these capabilities' on the network, and clients can ask 'give me an RSIP server that supports tunneling over IP-IP' instead of being told 'use server X at address Y' by an administrator.

sections.title: How SLP Works for RSIP
sections.content:
SLP divides into three components: User Agents (UAs) that represent clients seeking a service, Service Agents (SAs) that advertise services, and optional Directory Agents (DAs) that collect service advertisements. For RSIP: (1) The RSIP server implements an SLP SA. (2) The SA constructs a service advertisement with URL 'service:rsip' and attributes defined by the template (Section 7). (3) If an SLP DA is found, the SA registers the advertisement; otherwise the SA responds directly to multicast queries. (4) When an RSIP client needs a server, the UA queries the DA or SA, optionally with attribute filters. (5) The client receives the server hostname/address and port, then initiates RSIP protocol negotiation.

SLP has advantages over static configuration: discovery is dynamic (only active servers are found), no third-party configuration is needed (servers advertise themselves), clients can filter by attributes (e.g., tunneling type or current load), and SLP scopes allow administrators to partition services logically.
sections.plainLanguage: SLP is like a bulletin board: RSIP servers post notices about themselves, clients read the bulletin board and pick a server, then talk directly to that server. If the server goes down, clients refresh the bulletin board and find another.

sections.title: Scopes for Network Provisioning
sections.content:
An SLP scope is a named set of service advertisements that administrators use to control which clients see which services. By assigning clients and servers to specific scopes, administrators can ensure that, for example, clients in one subnet only discover RSIP servers designated for that subnet. Scopes are not access control (a client outside the scope can still reach a service in the scope if it knows the address); they simply govern SLP discovery.

For RSIP, scopes allow administrators to tie clients to specific realms via DHCP scope configuration. When a client is assigned an IP address and scope via DHCP, it will only discover RSIP servers in that scope. If an administrator needs to move clients from one realm to another, they can simply change the DHCP address assignment and scope, effectively redirecting all clients at once without manual intervention on each machine.
sections.plainLanguage: Scopes are like assigning people to different phone books. Clients in scope 'building-A' only see servers advertised in building-A's scope, so administrators can control which servers each group of clients uses.

sections.title: Load Balancing and Server Selection
sections.content:
SLP itself provides no built-in load balancing, but the RSIP service template includes a 'load' attribute (an integer 0-100) that allows RSIP servers to report their current utilization. Clients seeking the least-loaded server can perform the following: (1) Issue an SLP service request and collect all returned service URLs. (2) For each URL, request its 'load' attribute. (3) Sort by load and select the URL with the lowest number. (4) Establish an RSIP session with that server.

Because of network delays, this procedure does not guarantee finding the absolute lightest-loaded server, but provides a high probability that the selected server is relatively lightly loaded at the time of selection. Servers must update their service advertisements periodically as new connections arrive and are released to keep load information current.
sections.plainLanguage: Each RSIP server tells clients 'I am currently handling N connections.' Clients can ask for the load of each server and pick the one handling the fewest connections.

sections.title: The RSIP Service Type Template
sections.content:
The template defines the 'service:rsip' service type with the following attributes:

ipsec-support (Boolean, optional): whether the server supports IPsec. ike-support (Boolean, optional): whether the server supports IKE (Internet Key Exchange). tunnel-type (String, optional, multivalued): the tunneling methods supported, drawn from IP-IP, L2TP, GRE, or NONE. Default is IP-IP. A server can support multiple tunnel types. transport (String, optional, multivalued): the transport protocol used by RSIP itself, either TCP or UDP. Default is TCP. load (Integer, optional): from 0 to 100 indicating current server utilization.

These attributes allow clients to express specific requirements: 'I need an RSIP server supporting L2TP tunneling over UDP with low current load.' The template provides the standardized vocabulary for these negotiations.
sections.plainLanguage: The template is like a checklist: does the server support IPsec? What tunneling methods? What is its current workload? Clients can ask for servers matching any combination of these criteria.
